claims.text: Wear resistance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by lattice distortion.
High lattice distortion enhances dislocation pinning.
Dislocation hindrance minimizes plastic deformation during wear.
Thermal annealing can reduce lattice distortion in the coating.
Reduced lattice distortion lowers dislocation pinning.
Decreased hardness increases plastic deformation under wear conditions.
Increased plastic deformation produces a higher wear rate.
As-deposited high-entropy-alloy coatings exhibit high lattice distortion and a microstructure that promotes dislocation pinning.
Annealed coatings will have lower hardness than otherwise equivalent as-deposited coatings.
Annealed coatings will have a higher wear rate than otherwise equivalent as-deposited coatings.
As-deposited coatings have high hardness and lower wear rates because of effective dislocation pinning.
The proposed relationship should hold for coatings with similar compositions and microstructures when annealing changes lattice distortion without significant grain growth or phase transformation.
X-ray-diffraction peak broadening can be used to assess lattice distortion in these coatings.
TEM observations can be used to assess dislocation density in these coatings.

contradictions.description: The boundary limits the hypothesis to cases where annealing actually alters lattice distortion without major confounding changes, but the falsification rule treats failure of annealing to reduce lattice distortion as falsification. Such a result would instead show that the intervention failed to manipulate the proposed mediator and would not decisively test the mechanism.
